title: Churros
subtitle: fried choux pastry sticks with cinnamon sugar
excerpt: Churros are crisp fried dough sticks coated in cinnamon sugar. They are quick to make and best eaten warm, straight from the pan. Serve with thick hot chocolate for dipping.
sourceNotes: Churros are believed to have been brought to Spain by Portuguese sailors who encountered a similar fried dough in China. They became a popular street food throughout Spain and spread across Latin America with Spanish colonists. Mexican churros are thicker than Spanish ones and typically coated in cinnamon sugar.

glossaryTerms.definition: A light pastry made by cooking flour in water and butter on the hob, then beating in eggs. The high moisture content creates steam during cooking, which puffs the pastry from the inside.

content.text: This recipe makes 20 churros and takes around 35 minutes from start to finish. The dough is a basic
cooked on the hob, piped straight into hot oil and rolled in cinnamon sugar while still warm. Serve alongside thick hot chocolate for dipping if you like.

Use a large star nozzle in your piping bag for churros with the classic ridged surface. The ridges increase the surface area and give you more crunch per bite. Keep the oil at a steady 180C and fry in small batches so the temperature does not drop. A cooking thermometer is the most reliable way to monitor this.

items.prepNote: for frying, enough to fill pan to 5cm depth

content.text: Combine 300ml water and the butter in a large saucepan. Heat over a medium hob until the butter has melted and the water reaches a full rolling boil.

Remove the pan from the heat. Add all the flour at once and beat vigorously with a wooden spoon until a smooth dough forms and pulls away from the sides of the pan. Return to a low heat and stir for 1 minute to dry the dough slightly.

Leave the dough to cool for 5 minutes. Beat in the eggs one at a time, mixing thoroughly after each addition until the dough is smooth and glossy. It will look split at first but will come together with persistent beating.
Spoon the dough into a piping bag fitted with a large star nozzle. Pour enough vegetable oil into a large saucepan to reach 5cm up the sides. Heat to 180C on a cooking thermometer.
Mix the caster sugar and ground cinnamon in a shallow bowl. Set aside near the hob.
Pipe 10cm lengths of dough directly into the hot oil, snipping each one off with scissors. Fry 4 or 5 at a time for 3 to 4 minutes, turning once, until deep golden brown all over.
Lift the churros out with a slotted spoon and drain briefly on kitchen paper. While still hot, roll them in the cinnamon sugar until well coated. Serve immediately.

attrs.symptom: Churros burst open or fall apart in the oil
attrs.cause: The dough was too wet, or the eggs were added before the dough had cooled enough, causing it to split
attrs.fix: Let the dough cool for at least 5 minutes before adding eggs. The finished dough should hold a stiff peak when pulled with a spoon. If it looks runny, the dough absorbed too much moisture during cooking.

attrs.symptom: Churros are golden outside but raw and doughy in the centre
attrs.cause: The oil was too hot, cooking the outside quickly while the inside stayed raw
attrs.fix: Keep the oil at a steady 180C. If the oil is too hot the outside browns before the inside cooks through. Use a thermometer and fry in small batches to maintain the temperature.

attrs.symptom: Churros are greasy and heavy rather than crisp
attrs.cause: The oil temperature dropped too low, causing the churros to absorb oil rather than fry
attrs.fix: Fry no more than 4 or 5 churros at a time. Adding too many at once cools the oil rapidly. Let the oil return to 180C between batches before adding the next round.

content.text: Churros are sold by street vendors across Mexico and Spain. You find them at markets, fairs and roadside stalls. In Mexico they are often eaten as a morning snack or an afternoon treat. They are best fresh and hot, eaten standing up.
